title: Dynamic contribution by aquatic metabolism to carbon dioxide emissions from a low‐land mixed land‐use catchment
content:
Abstract

Carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions from streams are globally significant despite their limited areal extent and rival those from terrestrial ecosystems. Agricultural land represents 40% of the world's landmass; still, the magnitude and source dynamics of CO2 emissions from streams draining agricultural-influenced landscapes are poorly understood. We used high-frequency measurements of CO2 and dissolved oxygen in a temperate low-land mixed land-use catchment (21% agricultural) to estimate emissions and the contribution of in-stream metabolism. Although CO2 concentrations were high (median 3520 μatm), emissions were relatively low (median 4.0 g C m2 day−1) due to consistently low gas transfer velocities (k 600). In-stream metabolism accounted for 46% of the emissions on average, which was higher than expected for a third-order stream. Emissions peaked during late summer despite low k 600. Emissions were instead driven by high CO2 concentrations, highlighting the importance of CO2 supply over physical drivers. We show that low-elevation human-impacted streams exhibit distinct emission dynamics, underscoring the need to account for biological drivers in carbon budgets for these landscapes.
